script.opening: “I paid for a full health MOT and it’s flagged nine things in red. I need you to go through every one, refer me to a liver specialist and a hormone clinic, and I’d like it repeated on the NHS every three months to keep an eye on it.”

facts.text: Online company, finger-prick kit, posted at 4pm on a weekday, not fasting. 36 markers. The report flags nine results red with phrases like “seek medical advice”.
Desk job, drives everywhere, no exercise. About 20 units a week (beer at weekends, wine midweek). Takeaways three times a week. Stopped smoking 5 years ago (20 pack-years). Sleeps badly, snores.

facts.topic: Only if asked what prompted the test
facts.text: His brother Mark, 50, had a heart attack three months ago and had a stent. Their father died of a stroke at 64. Paul has been lying awake worrying he is next.

Brief tightness in his chest at night when he is worrying, lasting a minute or two, settles when he calms down. Never on exertion: walks up stairs and to the station without symptoms. No breathlessness, palpitations, fainting or sweating.
Tired, which he blames on poor sleep. Libido fine. No erectile difficulty. No jaundice, no abdominal pain. No urinary symptoms.
None prescribed. Bought a “testosterone booster” supplement online last month after seeing the result. No vitamin D yet.

Organised and slightly demanding, with the printout in hand. Irritated if told the results “don’t matter”. Softens and becomes emotional when asked about his brother. Accepts prioritisation if it is clearly about his heart risk and he has a concrete plan.

ice.ideas: “The red flags mean something’s wrong with my liver and my hormones.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA: his brother’s heart attack at 50 and his father’s stroke; he is frightened he will have a heart attack and has been getting anxiety-related chest tightness at night.
ice.expectations: “Go through all nine, refer to a liver specialist and a hormone clinic, vitamin D on prescription, repeat every three months.”

cues: “Every three months to keep an eye on it” — anxiety driving testing; ask what prompted it.
Lipids, HbA1c, BMI, BP 146/92 and an ex-smoker — the cardiovascular picture matters most.
A testosterone booster bought online — the harm of acting on an unreliable result.
PSA included without counselling — the downside of panels.

checkpoints.text: Acknowledges the effort and anxiety behind the private test, and explains the approach: the GP will act on clinically significant results, but will not repeat private panels routinely
Asks what prompted the test and uncovers the brother’s heart attack at 50 and his own night-time chest tightness; screens for features of angina or other cardiac symptoms

Prioritises cardiovascular risk: confirms blood pressure (home or ambulatory readings), repeats lipids and HbA1c, calculates QRISK3 including family history of premature CVD, and discusses lifestyle and statin therapy in line with NICE NG238

Assesses the raised ALT: repeat venous LFTs, a liver screen (hepatitis serology, iron studies), FIB-4 to stratify fibrosis risk, and alcohol use (AUDIT-C), considering fatty liver (MASLD) as the likely cause
Checks transferrin saturation for the raised ferritin (likely inflammatory or fatty liver, but haemochromatosis to be excluded)

Explains why an afternoon finger-prick testosterone and an isolated hs-CRP are not actionable, advises stopping the testosterone booster, and offers a properly timed morning test only if symptoms of hypogonadism develop
Advises self-care vitamin D supplementation; explains that the PSA was done without counselling but is normal; signposts lifestyle support (weight, alcohol, activity, sleep)
Agrees a prioritised plan with timelines and a follow-up appointment, and safety-nets for exertional or prolonged chest pain (999)

worked.txt: “I’m glad you’ve shared these. My job is to pick out what really matters for your health and act on that. Some of these flags are less important than they look. And we don’t repeat private panels every three months, but I will check the things that need checking.”
“Can I ask what made you decide to get this test done now?”
“That must have been a real shock, and I can see why you’re worried. So let’s focus on your heart and stroke risk first, because that’s what these results are really telling us about.”

“Your cholesterol, sugar, weight, blood pressure and your brother’s heart attack all add up. I’ll work out your ten-year risk properly, and we’ll talk about a statin and the changes that make the biggest difference.”
“The liver test is most likely fat in the liver, which goes with the same picture. I’ll repeat it properly with a few extra checks and a score that tells us whether you need a specialist.”

f.learning: People increasingly bring results from private, direct-to-consumer blood panels. GMC guidance is that doctors must act on clinically significant information, whatever its source, but the NHS is not obliged to repeat private screening tests on request or provide follow-up for every flagged marker. The skill is prioritisation. Panels flag results that are statistically outside a range rather than clinically important, may use unsuitable samples (finger-prick, non-fasting, afternoon testosterone) and include tests that need counselling (PSA). Here the important signal is cardiovascular: raised non-HDL cholesterol, low HDL, high triglycerides, non-diabetic hyperglycaemia, obesity, raised blood pressure, ex-smoking and a brother with a heart attack at 50, which is a family history of premature CVD that QRISK3 includes. NICE NG238 (2023) recommends formal risk assessment with QRISK3, lifestyle advice, and offering atorvastatin for primary prevention when risk is 10% or more, after confirming lipids. Blood pressure should be confirmed with home or ambulatory monitoring (NICE NG136). A raised ALT with metabolic risk factors is most often metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD, previously NAFLD): repeat venous LFTs, a liver aetiology screen, assess alcohol, and use FIB-4 (with ELF if indeterminate) to decide on referral (NICE NG49). Raised ferritin is commonly inflammatory or metabolic, but transferrin saturation excludes haemochromatosis. HbA1c 42–47 mmol/mol is non-diabetic hyperglycaemia (NICE PH38): repeat annually and offer the NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme. Vitamin D supplementation is a self-care purchase for most adults. An isolated hs-CRP and an afternoon testosterone without symptoms are not actionable. The hidden agenda, fear after a sibling’s heart attack, explains the demand for repeated testing; addressing it directly and channelling it into risk reduction is the heart of the consultation.

knowledge.summary: A private finger-prick panel with nine flags. What matters: a high cardiovascular risk profile with premature CVD in his brother, raised BP, likely fatty liver, non-diabetic hyperglycaemia and a raised ferritin needing transferrin saturation. What does not: afternoon testosterone, isolated hs-CRP, routine repeat panels. Vitamin D is self-care; the uncounselled PSA is normal. His brother’s heart attack is the hidden driver.

points.t: Act on clinically significant results whatever the source; explain what will and will not be followed up; the NHS does not repeat private screening panels on request [5].
QRISK3 (includes family history of CVD in a first-degree relative under 60). Repeat lipids; offer lifestyle advice and discuss atorvastatin if 10-year risk is 10% or more [1].
Clinic or pharmacy reading of 140/90 or more needs confirmation with home or ambulatory monitoring [2].
Repeat venous LFTs; liver screen (hepatitis B and C, iron studies, autoimmune if indicated); alcohol (AUDIT-C); FIB-4 to stratify fibrosis risk, ELF or specialist if indeterminate or high [3].
Often raised with fatty liver, alcohol or inflammation. Check transferrin saturation to exclude haemochromatosis.
Non-diabetic hyperglycaemia. Confirm, then annual HbA1c and referral to the NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme [4].
Afternoon or finger-prick testosterone is unreliable; test at 9–11am only if symptoms. Isolated hs-CRP does not guide management. Vitamin D: self-care supplement.
PSA testing should follow informed discussion. A normal result needs no action but explain its limits [6].

Idea (liver and hormone problems), concern (heart attack like his brother), expectation (referrals, vitamin D, repeat panels).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.

Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.

Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Paul, I’m Dr Clarke. I’ve got the report you uploaded. What would you like from today?

I paid for a full health MOT and it’s flagged nine things in red. I need you to go through every one, refer me to a liver specialist and a hormone clinic, and I’d like it repeated on the NHS every three months to keep an eye on it.

Thanks for sharing it. My job is to pick out what really matters for your health and act on that. Some of these flags are more important than others. Before we start, can I ask what made you decide to get tested now?
(pause) My brother had a heart attack three months ago. He’s 50. My dad died of a stroke. I keep lying awake thinking I’m next.
That must have been a real shock. I can see why you’re worried. Have you had any chest pain or tightness yourself?
Sometimes at night when I’m worrying, a tight feeling for a minute or two. Never when I’m walking or on the stairs.
Any breathlessness, palpitations, sweating or blackouts? Does it ever come on with effort?
No. Never with effort.
That pattern sounds much more like worry than your heart, but I’ll keep it in mind. How much do you drink in a week, and do you smoke?
About 20 units. Stopped smoking five years ago.

Here’s how I read your results. The most important message is about your heart and stroke risk: your cholesterol pattern, the borderline sugar, your weight, the blood pressure at the pharmacy, and your brother’s heart attack all add up. That’s where I want to focus.
So it’s my heart, not my liver?

They’re linked. The liver test is most likely fat in the liver, which goes with the same picture. I’ll repeat it with a proper blood sample, add some checks for other causes, and use a score that tells us whether you need a liver specialist. Your iron store is a bit high, often from the same thing, but I’ll add one test to rule out an inherited iron condition.
And the testosterone?

That was taken at 4pm, when levels are naturally lower, and you don’t have symptoms of it being low. I wouldn’t act on it. I’d stop the booster, as we don’t know what’s in those. The inflammation marker on its own doesn’t tell us anything useful. Vitamin D is worth taking, but it’s something you buy, it’s cheap.
There was a PSA in there too.
It’s normal. Ideally that test is done after a conversation about its pros and cons, because it can give false alarms. If you’d like that conversation in future, we can have it.

So the plan: a fasting blood test with cholesterol, sugar, liver tests, a liver screen and the iron test; a home blood pressure monitor for a week; then I’ll calculate your ten-year heart risk properly, including your brother. We’ll talk about a statin, which is likely to be recommended, and the changes that make the biggest difference: alcohol, weight and walking. Your sugar result means you can join a free NHS programme too.
What about every three months?

We won’t repeat the whole panel, because most of it won’t change what we do. But I’ll check the important things at the right intervals, and see you in three weeks with the results. That’s a better way to keep an eye on you.
Can you tell me the plan back?
Bloods, home blood pressure, heart risk score, probably a statin. Liver score. Stop the booster, buy vitamin D. Cut the beer. See you in three weeks.
Exactly. If you get chest pain that comes on with effort, lasts more than a few minutes, or comes with breathlessness, sweating or feeling faint, call 999.
